results.taskOutput:
I deployed the canary and updated the Service to split traffic roughly 50/50.

What I did:
- Created Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
    - containerPort: 80 (matches stable)
    - Same security configuration as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - This targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1 pods
  - Kept port settings as-is: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged from stable)

Result:
- With 2 pods in engine-v2-0 and 2 pods in engine-v2-1 behind the same Service, kube-proxy will distribute connections approximately evenly, yielding ~50% traffic to the canary.

Notes and quick adjustments:
- To shift traffic, adjust replica counts between the two Deployments (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- To roll back quickly to stable-only routing, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  annotations:

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

I deployed the canary and updated the Service to split traffic roughly 50/50.

What I did:
- Created Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
    - containerPort: 80 (matches stable)
    - Same security configuration as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - This targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1 pods
  - Kept port settings as-is: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged from stable)

Result:
- With 2 pods in engine-v2-0 and 2 pods in engine-v2-1 behind the same Service, kube-proxy will distribute connections approximately evenly, yielding ~50% traffic to the canary.

Notes and quick adjustments:
- To shift traffic, adjust replica counts between the two Deployments (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- To roll back quickly to stable-only routing, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

outputSteps.content:
I deployed the canary and updated the Service to split traffic roughly 50/50.

What I did:
- Created Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine
    - containerPort: 80 (matches stable)
    - Same security configuration as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine
  - This targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1 pods
  - Kept port settings as-is: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (unchanged from stable)

Result:
- With 2 pods in engine-v2-0 and 2 pods in engine-v2-1 behind the same Service, kube-proxy will distribute connections approximately evenly, yielding ~50% traffic to the canary.

Notes and quick adjustments:
- To shift traffic, adjust replica counts between the two Deployments (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- To roll back quickly to stable-only routing, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.

Steps.message:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The Deployment pod was starting with command: ["/bin/sh","-c"] and args: ["nonexistent_command"], which caused immediate exits and BackOff.
- Change made: Cleared the custom command/args so the container uses the image’s default entrypoint (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged).
- Result: A new ReplicaSet was rolled out and the pod is healthy.
  - Running pod: app-57fc6cc69b-cd54j
  - Status: 1/1 Running
  - Container logs show NGINX started successfully.

If you intended to run a custom startup command, let me know what it should be (and ensure it exists in the image). For example, to run NGINX in the foreground you can set command: ["nginx"] and args: ["-g","daemon off;"].

Fixed.

- Root cause: The Deployment pod was starting with command: ["/bin/sh","-c"] and args: ["nonexistent_command"], which caused immediate exits and BackOff.
- Change made: Cleared the custom command/args so the container uses the image’s default entrypoint (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged).
- Result: A new ReplicaSet was rolled out and the pod is healthy.
  - Running pod: app-57fc6cc69b-cd54j
  - Status: 1/1 Running
  - Container logs show NGINX started successfully.

If you intended to run a custom startup command, let me know what it should be (and ensure it exists in the image). For example, to run NGINX in the foreground you can set command: ["nginx"] and args: ["-g","daemon off;"].

- Updated the container image to a valid tag: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest

Verification

- kubectl -n debug rollout status deploy/app

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC used a non-existent StorageClass "sc". The scheduler reported “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims”.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc (it had no volume/data yet).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with a valid StorageClass: standard (the default in this cluster).

Current status
- homepage-pod in namespace homepage-ns is Running and Ready.
- The PVC was provisioned successfully and bound to a new PV.

If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc) or want me to make one of them the cluster default, let me know and I can adjust it.

I found and fixed two misconfigurations that kept your webapp unhealthy:

What was wrong
- The container (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were checking http://:80 on non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready).
  - The Service targetPort was 80, so traffic never reached the app.
- Result: probes failed and the app wasn’t reachable via the Service.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Probes now use path “/” on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service:
  - targetPort updated to 8080 (Service continues to serve on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is healthy and Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are populated and point to the pod on port 8080.
- I verified the app responds with the default nginx welcome page from inside the pod.

How you can verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy webapp
- kubectl -n orders get pods -o wide
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- Optionally, test locally: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer) or a custom health check path, tell me your preference and I’ll set it up.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed two misconfigurations that kept your webapp unhealthy:

What was wrong
- The container (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Liveness/readiness probes were checking http://:80 on non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready).
  - The Service targetPort was 80, so traffic never reached the app.
- Result: probes failed and the app wasn’t reachable via the Service.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Probes now use path “/” on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Service:
  - targetPort updated to 8080 (Service continues to serve on port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is healthy and Ready (1/1).
- Service endpoints are populated and point to the pod on port 8080.
- I verified the app responds with the default nginx welcome page from inside the pod.

How you can verify
- kubectl -n orders get deploy webapp
- kubectl -n orders get pods -o wide
- kubectl -n orders get svc webapp
- Optionally, test locally: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer) or a custom health check path, tell me your preference and I’ll set it up.

Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup did not grant permissions on pods. It only allowed listing apps/deployments, so the pod-reader ServiceAccount couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role to include permissions on core/pods:
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- Kept the existing permission on apps/deployments.

Current state
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount can now list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.
- Note: there are currently no pods in that namespace, so a successful list will return empty.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods -n simple-rbac-setup
  Expected: yes
- kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader get pods -n simple-rbac-setup
  Expected: No resources found in simple-rbac-setup namespace.

If you want this ServiceAccount to read pods in other namespaces as well, we can either:
- Bind a ClusterRole (e.g., view or a custom cluster-wide pod-read role) via a RoleBinding in each namespace, or
- Use a ClusterRoleBinding (grants across all namespaces).

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup did not grant permissions on pods. It only allowed listing apps/deployments, so the pod-reader ServiceAccount couldn’t list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role to include permissions on core/pods:
  - resources: ["pods"]
  - verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- Kept the existing permission on apps/deployments.

Current state
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount can now list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.
- Note: there are currently no pods in that namespace, so a successful list will return empty.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader list pods -n simple-rbac-setup
  Expected: yes
- kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader get pods -n simple-rbac-setup
  Expected: No resources found in simple-rbac-setup namespace.

If you want this ServiceAccount to read pods in other namespaces as well, we can either:
- Bind a ClusterRole (e.g., view or a custom cluster-wide pod-read role) via a RoleBinding in each namespace, or
- Use a ClusterRoleBinding (grants across all namespaces).

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
I found two misconfigurations on the nginx Service in namespace web that made it unreachable:

- Service selector mismatch: Service selector was app=web, but the Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- Wrong targetPort: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Service targeted port 80.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods: app=nginx
- Updated the Service targetPort to 8080 (Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster)

Current state (verified)
- Endpoints now exist: 10.244.0.26:8080
- In-cluster access works: curl to nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80 returns HTTP 200

Notes
- There are no NetworkPolicies or Ingress objects blocking traffic in web.
- The Service type is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - Change it to a NodePort or LoadBalancer Service, or
  - Create an Ingress (preferred if you have an ingress controller).

Would you like me to expose it externally (Ingress or NodePort/LoadBalancer)? If so, tell me which option you prefer.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

I found two misconfigurations on the nginx Service in namespace web that made it unreachable:

- Service selector mismatch: Service selector was app=web, but the Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- Wrong targetPort: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Service targeted port 80.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods: app=nginx
- Updated the Service targetPort to 8080 (Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster)

Current state (verified)
- Endpoints now exist: 10.244.0.26:8080
- In-cluster access works: curl to nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80 returns HTTP 200

Notes
- There are no NetworkPolicies or Ingress objects blocking traffic in web.
- The Service type is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - Change it to a NodePort or LoadBalancer Service, or
  - Create an Ingress (preferred if you have an ingress controller).

Would you like me to expose it externally (Ingress or NodePort/LoadBalancer)? If so, tell me which option you prefer.

outputSteps.content:
I found two misconfigurations on the nginx Service in namespace web that made it unreachable:

- Service selector mismatch: Service selector was app=web, but the Deployment/Pods are labeled app=nginx, so the Service had no endpoints.
- Wrong targetPort: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Service targeted port 80.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to match the Pods: app=nginx
- Updated the Service targetPort to 8080 (Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster)

Current state (verified)
- Endpoints now exist: 10.244.0.26:8080
- In-cluster access works: curl to nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80 returns HTTP 200

Notes
- There are no NetworkPolicies or Ingress objects blocking traffic in web.
- The Service type is ClusterIP, so it’s accessible only inside the cluster. If you need external access, I can:
  - Change it to a NodePort or LoadBalancer Service, or
  - Create an Ingress (preferred if you have an ingress controller).

Would you like me to expose it externally (Ingress or NodePort/LoadBalancer)? If so, tell me which option you prefer.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Root cause 1 (pods Pending): The web-app Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Root cause 2 (connection refused): The Service was targeting port 80, while the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default. Even once pods run, sending traffic to targetPort 80 would be refused.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Corrected ports:
  - Set containerPort to 8080 in the Deployment.
  - Set Service targetPort to 8080 (kept Service port 80 for backward compatibility).

Current status
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Running and Available.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service points to the pods on targetPort 8080.

Why this fixes it
- Removing the nodeSelector allowed pods to start, creating Service endpoints.
- Aligning targetPort with the container’s actual listening port (8080) prevents connection refused.

How to verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,po,svc
- Test in-cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -it --rm -- sh -lc 'curl -sI web-app-service | head -n1'
  - Expected: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
- Or port-forward to your machine:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward svc/web-app-service 8080:80
  - Then browse http://localhost:8080

If you intended to pin to GPU nodes
- Either restore the nodeSelector and label a suitable node:
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or use a toleration/affinity that matches your node labeling scheme.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Reinstate a nodeSelector once the proper node is labeled.
- Add a readinessProbe and livenessProbe to harden the Deployment.

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings
- Root cause 1 (pods Pending): The web-app Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Root cause 2 (connection refused): The Service was targeting port 80, while the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default. Even once pods run, sending traffic to targetPort 80 would be refused.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Corrected ports:
  - Set containerPort to 8080 in the Deployment.
  - Set Service targetPort to 8080 (kept Service port 80 for backward compatibility).

Current status
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Running and Available.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service points to the pods on targetPort 8080.

Why this fixes it
- Removing the nodeSelector allowed pods to start, creating Service endpoints.
- Aligning targetPort with the container’s actual listening port (8080) prevents connection refused.

How to verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,po,svc
- Test in-cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -it --rm -- sh -lc 'curl -sI web-app-service | head -n1'
  - Expected: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
- Or port-forward to your machine:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward svc/web-app-service 8080:80
  - Then browse http://localhost:8080

If you intended to pin to GPU nodes
- Either restore the nodeSelector and label a suitable node:
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or use a toleration/affinity that matches your node labeling scheme.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Reinstate a nodeSelector once the proper node is labeled.
- Add a readinessProbe and livenessProbe to harden the Deployment.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Root cause 1 (pods Pending): The web-app Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Root cause 2 (connection refused): The Service was targeting port 80, while the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default. Even once pods run, sending traffic to targetPort 80 would be refused.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Corrected ports:
  - Set containerPort to 8080 in the Deployment.
  - Set Service targetPort to 8080 (kept Service port 80 for backward compatibility).

Current status
- Deployment webshop-frontend/web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Running and Available.
- Service webshop-frontend/web-app-service points to the pods on targetPort 8080.

Why this fixes it
- Removing the nodeSelector allowed pods to start, creating Service endpoints.
- Aligning targetPort with the container’s actual listening port (8080) prevents connection refused.

How to verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,po,svc
- Test in-cluster:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -it --rm -- sh -lc 'curl -sI web-app-service | head -n1'
  - Expected: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
- Or port-forward to your machine:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend port-forward svc/web-app-service 8080:80
  - Then browse http://localhost:8080

If you intended to pin to GPU nodes
- Either restore the nodeSelector and label a suitable node:
  - kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or use a toleration/affinity that matches your node labeling scheme.

Let me know if you want me to:
- Reinstate a nodeSelector once the proper node is labeled.
- Add a readinessProbe and livenessProbe to harden the Deployment.

- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, serving on port 8080
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox, running tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log

- Pod phase: Running
- ContainersReady/Ready: True for both containers

Optional verifications:
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod

Steps.message:
Done. I created the Pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace with:

- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, serving on port 8080
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox, running tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Readiness: readinessProbe on web-server (HTTP GET / on port 8080), so the Pod is considered Ready when the web server serves traffic

Current state:
- Pod phase: Running
- ContainersReady/Ready: True for both containers

Optional verifications:
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging logs communication-pod -c logger (send a few requests first to generate access logs)
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging exec -c web-server communication-pod -- wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080/

The secure multi-tenant development environment has been created with namespacing, RBAC, quotas, and network isolation as requested. Summary of what’s been applied and how it meets your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to support network policies:
  - dev-* namespaces: env=dev, access-scope=developer, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: env=dev, access-scope=shared
  - staging: env=staging, access-scope=restricted
  - prod: env=prod, access-scope=restricted

2) RBAC
- Per-developer namespaces: each user and their service account get full access (ClusterRole edit) to their own namespace
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding developer-edit -> subjects: User alice, SA dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding developer-edit -> subjects: User bob, SA dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding developer-edit -> subjects: User charlie, SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- dev-shared: read-only (ClusterRole view) for all three users and their service accounts via RoleBinding dev-shared-viewers
- staging/prod: no developer RoleBindings created (access is implicitly only for cluster admins per least-privilege)

3) Service Accounts
- Created: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Each SA has:
  - Full access to its own namespace (via RoleBinding above)
  - Read-only access to dev-shared (via RoleBinding in dev-shared)

4) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

5) Network Policies (isolation + least privilege)
- Default deny (ingress and egress) in all six namespaces
- Allow intra-namespace traffic (ingress and egress) in each namespace
- Allow DNS egress to kube-dns/CoreDNS in kube-system (UDP/TCP 53) in each namespace
- Dev namespace interactions:
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow egress to dev-shared and ingress from dev-shared
  - In dev-shared: allow ingress from namespaces labeled env=dev, access-scope=developer (i.e., the dev-* namespaces)
- Result:
  - Cross-developer traffic (e.g., dev-alice to dev-bob) is blocked
  - Developers can communicate within their own namespace and with dev-shared
  - staging and prod are isolated from dev namespaces (only same-namespace traffic + DNS allowed)

Notes and validation
- Principle of least privilege:
  - Developers get edit in their own namespace only; view only in dev-shared; no access to staging/prod
  - NetworkPolicies default-deny everything and allow only minimum required paths
- If any workloads in these namespaces must call the Kubernetes API (kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add an allow-egress-to-API policy (requires using an IPBlock to the Service IP of “kubernetes” or your control plane endpoints). Let me know if you want me to add that.
- Quick validation ideas:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-bob get pods -> no
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-alice create deploy -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared get pods -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared create deploy -> no
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-bob -> should fail
  - From a pod in dev-alice, dig or nslookup via 10.96.0.10 or kube-dns -> should succeed
  - From a pod in staging/prod, attempts to reach dev-* namespaces should fail

Would you like me to:
- Add a LimitRange in each namespace to set default requests/limits (helps enforce quotas predictably)?
- Add an egress rule to allow pods to reach the Kubernetes API server if needed by your applications?
- Create kubeconfigs or tokens for the developer service accounts (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)?

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

The secure multi-tenant development environment has been created with namespacing, RBAC, quotas, and network isolation as requested. Summary of what’s been applied and how it meets your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to support network policies:
  - dev-* namespaces: env=dev, access-scope=developer, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: env=dev, access-scope=shared
  - staging: env=staging, access-scope=restricted
  - prod: env=prod, access-scope=restricted

2) RBAC
- Per-developer namespaces: each user and their service account get full access (ClusterRole edit) to their own namespace
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding developer-edit -> subjects: User alice, SA dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding developer-edit -> subjects: User bob, SA dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding developer-edit -> subjects: User charlie, SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- dev-shared: read-only (ClusterRole view) for all three users and their service accounts via RoleBinding dev-shared-viewers
- staging/prod: no developer RoleBindings created (access is implicitly only for cluster admins per least-privilege)

3) Service Accounts
- Created: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Each SA has:
  - Full access to its own namespace (via RoleBinding above)
  - Read-only access to dev-shared (via RoleBinding in dev-shared)

4) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

5) Network Policies (isolation + least privilege)
- Default deny (ingress and egress) in all six namespaces
- Allow intra-namespace traffic (ingress and egress) in each namespace
- Allow DNS egress to kube-dns/CoreDNS in kube-system (UDP/TCP 53) in each namespace
- Dev namespace interactions:
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow egress to dev-shared and ingress from dev-shared
  - In dev-shared: allow ingress from namespaces labeled env=dev, access-scope=developer (i.e., the dev-* namespaces)
- Result:
  - Cross-developer traffic (e.g., dev-alice to dev-bob) is blocked
  - Developers can communicate within their own namespace and with dev-shared
  - staging and prod are isolated from dev namespaces (only same-namespace traffic + DNS allowed)

Notes and validation
- Principle of least privilege:
  - Developers get edit in their own namespace only; view only in dev-shared; no access to staging/prod
  - NetworkPolicies default-deny everything and allow only minimum required paths
- If any workloads in these namespaces must call the Kubernetes API (kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add an allow-egress-to-API policy (requires using an IPBlock to the Service IP of “kubernetes” or your control plane endpoints). Let me know if you want me to add that.
- Quick validation ideas:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-bob get pods -> no
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-alice create deploy -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared get pods -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared create deploy -> no
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-bob -> should fail
  - From a pod in dev-alice, dig or nslookup via 10.96.0.10 or kube-dns -> should succeed
  - From a pod in staging/prod, attempts to reach dev-* namespaces should fail

Would you like me to:
- Add a LimitRange in each namespace to set default requests/limits (helps enforce quotas predictably)?
- Add an egress rule to allow pods to reach the Kubernetes API server if needed by your applications?
- Create kubeconfigs or tokens for the developer service accounts (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)?

The secure multi-tenant development environment has been created with namespacing, RBAC, quotas, and network isolation as requested. Summary of what’s been applied and how it meets your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled to support network policies:
  - dev-* namespaces: env=dev, access-scope=developer, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: env=dev, access-scope=shared
  - staging: env=staging, access-scope=restricted
  - prod: env=prod, access-scope=restricted

2) RBAC
- Per-developer namespaces: each user and their service account get full access (ClusterRole edit) to their own namespace
  - dev-alice: RoleBinding developer-edit -> subjects: User alice, SA dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob: RoleBinding developer-edit -> subjects: User bob, SA dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: RoleBinding developer-edit -> subjects: User charlie, SA dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- dev-shared: read-only (ClusterRole view) for all three users and their service accounts via RoleBinding dev-shared-viewers
- staging/prod: no developer RoleBindings created (access is implicitly only for cluster admins per least-privilege)

3) Service Accounts
- Created: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Each SA has:
  - Full access to its own namespace (via RoleBinding above)
  - Read-only access to dev-shared (via RoleBinding in dev-shared)

4) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu=2, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu=4, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu=8, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

5) Network Policies (isolation + least privilege)
- Default deny (ingress and egress) in all six namespaces
- Allow intra-namespace traffic (ingress and egress) in each namespace
- Allow DNS egress to kube-dns/CoreDNS in kube-system (UDP/TCP 53) in each namespace
- Dev namespace interactions:
  - In dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: allow egress to dev-shared and ingress from dev-shared
  - In dev-shared: allow ingress from namespaces labeled env=dev, access-scope=developer (i.e., the dev-* namespaces)
- Result:
  - Cross-developer traffic (e.g., dev-alice to dev-bob) is blocked
  - Developers can communicate within their own namespace and with dev-shared
  - staging and prod are isolated from dev namespaces (only same-namespace traffic + DNS allowed)

Notes and validation
- Principle of least privilege:
  - Developers get edit in their own namespace only; view only in dev-shared; no access to staging/prod
  - NetworkPolicies default-deny everything and allow only minimum required paths
- If any workloads in these namespaces must call the Kubernetes API (kubernetes.default.svc:443), we can add an allow-egress-to-API policy (requires using an IPBlock to the Service IP of “kubernetes” or your control plane endpoints). Let me know if you want me to add that.
- Quick validation ideas:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-bob get pods -> no
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-alice create deploy -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared get pods -> yes
  - kubectl auth can-i --as alice --namespace dev-shared create deploy -> no
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a service in dev-bob -> should fail
  - From a pod in dev-alice, dig or nslookup via 10.96.0.10 or kube-dns -> should succeed
  - From a pod in staging/prod, attempts to reach dev-* namespaces should fail

- Add a LimitRange in each namespace to set default requests/limits (helps enforce quotas predictably)?
- Add an egress rule to allow pods to reach the Kubernetes API server if needed by your applications?
- Create kubeconfigs or tokens for the developer service accounts (alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa)?

Done.

What I created
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) to provide stable identities for the StatefulSet
- StatefulSet: db with 3 replicas
  - volumeClaimTemplates: one 1Gi PVC per pod (name: data), mounted at /data
  - initContainer writes the file /data/test with the string initial_data only if it doesn’t already exist
  - main container: busybox sleeping (so the pods stay running)

Then I scaled the StatefulSet back down to 1 replica. The scale spec is set to 1; Kubernetes will reconcile from 3 to 1. The PVCs for ordinal 1 and 2 are retained, so data persists for db-1 and db-2 even after scale-down.

How to verify (optional)
- Pods: kubectl get pods -n statefulset-test -l app=db
- PVCs: kubectl get pvc -n statefulset-test
- File content (on remaining pod): kubectl exec -n statefulset-test db-0 -- sh -c 'cat /data/test'
- If you later scale up, db-1 and db-2 will reattach their original PVCs and still contain /data/test with initial_data.

What I created
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) to provide stable identities for the StatefulSet
- StatefulSet: db with 3 replicas
